prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength so that the lattice does not perturb the clock transition, bringing optical frequency standards to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, Katori and Ye, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. After the full exchange the case rests on three things that I can judge directly. First, the idea is an invention with a precise physical content: choosing the lattice wavelength so that the light shifts of the two clock states cancel lets many neutral atoms be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime without perturbing the transition. The comb of 2005 gave us a way to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, but neither introduced this scheme, and the citation I propose names it explicitly so that the prize cannot be read as a reward for clocks in general. Second, maturity is demonstrated by measurement and not by argument: independent laboratories with several species compare clocks at the 1e-18 level and the results agree, which is the strongest form of confirmation an instrument-led discovery can have. Third, the attribution is the only one on the shortlist where the supplied names map onto the idea and its decisive realisation without a first author or a principal claimant left outside. Katori carries the proposal and the first strontium lattice clock; Ye carried the technique to its present accuracy and stability and also opened the many-body and spin-correlation regime of lattice clocks, which is more than a number and which I would like the citation to reflect. Having read the other seven statements, I find that six members reach B007 for scientific reasons they state themselves, and I do not count that as a reason in its own right. What I take from the chair's questions is that B005 is the real alternative, and that is how I have tested my own position.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining reservation is that Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat, and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups, contributed substantially to making lattice clocks work, and a two-name prize leaves them outside. I accept that this is a genuine cost, but I do not think it changes the choice of laureates: the limit of three people makes an omission of this kind unavoidable in any collaborative field, and the credited pair are the ones whose contributions define the concept and its record realisation. The second reservation is the metrology lineage honoured in 2005 and 2012. I have addressed it by wording the citation around neutral-atom magic-wavelength trapping, but a reader who sees one lineage will still see one. The third is that the redefinition of the second has not happened. I consider that a prospective payoff and not a condition for the discovery, because the accuracy and reproducibility are already established, but it is a legitimate argument for patience and I do not dismiss it. Finally, I recognise that B005 is a larger field by number of researchers and that in a few years a better-resolved B005 may be an easier prize to defend than it is today.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B005) with MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero. He argues that the open pairing mechanism should not be a test of maturity because high-temperature superconductivity was recognised in 1987 without an agreed mechanism, and that three names are the accurate description of a prediction-plus-discovery story.
responses.response: The 1987 comparison is fair, and I accept that robust phenomenology can carry a prize without a settled mechanism; I no longer rest my objection on the mechanism alone. My difficulty is with the combination of an unsettled interpretation and a credit chain that cannot be completed. A 1987-type citation names the phenomenon and the people who found it, and here the first author of the 2018 papers, Cao, is not among the supplied names, while Dean, Young, Yazdani and the earlier band-theory work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto are also claimants. I take your point that the three-name limit is structural and that it would also bite on B007 if one were strict about Takamoto and Lemonde. But the difference is of degree: for the clocks the omitted contributors are parallel developers of a technique, while for B005 the omitted person carried out the key experiment. I also accept your reply on twist-angle disorder, which does not undermine the core phenomenology, and I accept that B005 is timely. My ordering of the two rests on attribution, not on a judgement that the physics is less important.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B007 with Katori and Ye, raises Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat as uncredited, and flags the repeated honouring of precision metrology (laser cooling 1997, combs 2005, ion control 2012) as the main risk to the case.
responses.response: I agree with the pairing and I want to answer the chair's question about her four names directly. None of Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde or Lisdat changes my view of a two-name prize. Takamoto belongs to Katori's own programme and the first strontium lattice clock is already in Katori's credit. Ludlow worked in Ye's laboratory in the record-accuracy period, which is Ye's credit. Lemonde and Lisdat built independent lattice clocks, and that independence is what supports the reproducibility argument; it does not make them co-inventors of the magic-wavelength scheme. On the metrology lineage, I would answer it with the citation and not with the argument: it should reward neutral-atom lattice trapping at a magic wavelength, which neither 1997, 2005 nor 2012 covered. I continue to hold, as in round 1, that adding a third name from the comb or ion-clock side would blur precisely that distinction.

responses.point: Pearce prefers B007 and says B005 is the natural strongest competitor but with a visible hole in the credit chain. He accepts the 2005 and 2012 overlap as a risk, does not favour B043 as a second part, and notes that B007 is a natural runner-up, not a wrongful choice, if the committee decides B005 is larger.
responses.response: I agree that the choice between B007 and B005 turns on attribution and timing and not on merit, and I accept your reading on atom interferometry. Chu already holds a prize for laser cooling and the 1991 priority is shared among several experiments, so B043 is not a candidate I would pair with the clocks, and I have kept it only as a distant alternative. I also accept that the chair's question about a two-part prize has a negative answer for this year on my reading: the only candidates I can see that are distinct from B007 in content have credit problems of their own (Cao in B005, four names for three places in B044, the collaboration size in B012), and a composite would also force the three-person limit across two parts, which would shorten the clock citation to one name or cut the second part. I therefore prefer a clean single part.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B025 to B007 and stresses that agreement between independent clocks at the 1e-18 level removes doubt about maturity, while noting that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened and that the uncredited contributions would be hard to defend.
responses.response: I welcome the point about independent intercomparisons, which is the main reason I regard maturity as demonstrated and not claimed. On your reservation about the pending redefinition, I would separate the discovery from its adoption: a redefinition is a metrological decision that depends on a roadmap and on international agreement, and it is not a test of whether the physics is correct. I agree that waiting is a legitimate position, but I note that your own argument for patience with B005, that a prize for the platform is easier to defend a few years from now, applies in some degree to B007 as well. I think it applies less, because the 1e-18 comparisons already exist. I would still ask that the citation not be reduced to a number. The many-body and spin-correlation results from Ye's laboratory are what make the clock a physics instrument and not only a better oscillator, and I would like the committee to see them as part of the credit.

uncertainties: How the committee weights the metrology lineage of 2005 and 2012 against the neutral-atom magic-wavelength invention; the citation wording is my attempt to separate them but it cannot remove the question.
Whether the omission of Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and Takamoto will be accepted as a consequence of the three-person limit or read as an unfair cut, and I cannot resolve this from the supplied names.
Whether B005 in a few years, with a better-resolved mechanism and a settled credit chain, would be the stronger prize; this year I judge the attribution gap decisive.
My assessment of priority history and of recent clock-comparison results rests on recalled history and not on verified records.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I spent part of my doctoral period in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's frequency-comb work is the background to the JILA programme where Jun Ye works. The profile documents no collaboration or co-authorship with Katori or Ye, so I do not propose recusal, but the committee should have it on record. I am also a quantum-optics and quantum-memory researcher, a field adjacent to atom interferometry (B043), which I now hold only as a distant alternative. Several of my Lund colleagues work in quantum information, but none has a documented role in any shortlisted candidate. I note that, as an atomic physicist, I am more likely to favour an AMO topic, and I ask colleagues to challenge that if they see it in my reasoning.
